title: Numbers, age & quantities
goal: Count things and people with the right classifier, ask how much and how many, give your age and use ordinals.
intro: Learn the numbers 0–100 from the **Numbers** chart — Odia numbers between 20 and 100 are irregular, so practise them in small groups (21–30, 31–40…). This unit shows how to use them: in Odia you rarely say just 'two mangoes'; you say *two-ṭi mangoes*, with a **classifier** in between.

vocab.note: Colloquial: ଗୋଟେ (goṭe). Used instead of ଏକ when counting objects.
ଦୁଇଟି ଆମ୍ବ 'two mangoes'; ବହିଟି 'the book'. Neutral/polite.
ଦୁଇଟା ଆମ୍ବ. More casual than ଟି; also used for clock time.

vocab.en: piece; classifier for sheets, cloth, flat things

vocab.note: In speech people often say 'number X' instead: ଦୁଇ ନମ୍ବର 'number two'.

phrases.en: This is my first time in Odisha.

grammar.title: Classifiers: ଟି, ଟା, ଜଣ, ଖଣ୍ଡ
grammar.body:
When you count nouns in Odia, a **classifier** goes between the number and the noun:

**-ଟି** (*-ṭi*) for things (neutral, polite): ଦୁଇଟି ଆମ୍ବ 'two mangoes'. 'One' is the special form **ଗୋଟିଏ**.
**-ଟା** (*-ṭa*) is the casual version: ଦୁଇଟା ଆମ୍ବ. (It can sound dismissive when used for people.)
**ଜଣ** (*jôṇô*) for people: ତିନି ଜଣ ଲୋକ. 'One person' is **ଜଣେ**.
**ଖଣ୍ଡ** (*khôṇḍô*) for flat things and pieces: ଦୁଇ ଖଣ୍ଡ କାଗଜ 'two sheets of paper'; 'one piece' is **ଖଣ୍ଡେ**.

Attached directly to a noun, ଟି/ଟା act like English **'the'**: ବହିଟି 'the book', ପିଲାଟି 'the child'. For plural 'the', use -ଗୁଡ଼ିକ / -ମାନେ (Unit 3).

examples.en: Give me two sheets of paper. (familiar)

grammar.title: Asking how many, how much, how old
grammar.body:
**କେତେ** (*kete*) asks 'how much / how many' in general; **କେତୋଟି** asks 'how many (things)' and **କେତେ ଜଣ** 'how many (people)'. Age is ବୟସ 'age': ଆପଣଙ୍କ ବୟସ କେତେ? 'Your age how-much?' — answer ମୋ ବୟସ … ବର୍ଷ.

Ordinals are Sanskrit words (ପ୍ରଥମ, ଦ୍ୱିତୀୟ, ତୃତୀୟ …) and come before the noun like adjectives. In casual speech people often use *number*: ତିନି ନମ୍ବର ବସ୍ 'bus number three', or the native form ପହିଲା (*pôhila*) 'first'.

examples.en: How many children do you have?
How many mangoes do you need?
I live on the third floor.

dialogue.title: Grandma's questions
dialogue.setting: Sam visits Lipi's family. Her grandmother (ଜେଜେମା) asks him questions over sweets.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ମୋ ବୟସ ଅଠାଇଶି ବର୍ଷ, ଜେଜେମା। ଆପଣଙ୍କ ବୟସ କେତେ?
lines.roman: mo bôyôsô ôṭhaisi bôrsô, jejema. apôṇôṅkô bôyôsô kete?
lines.en: I'm twenty-eight, Grandma. How old are you?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Eighty! How many children do you have?

lines.speaker: Jejema
lines.native: ଚାରି ଜଣ — ତିନି ପୁଅ, ଜଣେ ଝିଅ। ଲିପିର ବାପା ମୋର ପ୍ରଥମ ପୁଅ।
lines.roman: chari jôṇô — tini puô, jôṇe jhiô. Lipirô bapa morô prôthômô puô.
lines.en: Four — three sons and one daughter. Lipi's father is my first son.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: No, Grandma, it's already too much!

culture: Large numbers in India are grouped in **lakhs** (ଲକ୍ଷ, 1,00,000) and **crores** (କୋଟି, 1,00,00,000), not millions — prices and populations are always quoted this way. Odia numbers above 20 are irregular, and in fast speech many people (especially in towns) switch to English for phone numbers and prices; but older people, markets and radio still use Odia numbers. Asking someone's age is not considered rude.
